title: T1595 — Active Scanning
subtitle: Watch a full active-scan story against a small company network.
aria: Simulation. Step 1: Choose a target. The attacker picks a range owned by the company. Public registration records show the company uses 203.0.113.0/24, so the attacker writes down all 256 addresses.

steps.title: Choose a target
steps.caption: The attacker picks a range owned by the company. Public registration records show the company uses 203.0.113.0/24, so the attacker writes down all 256 addresses.
steps.defender: Nothing is attacking yet, so there is nothing to alert on. Make sure you keep an accurate list of the addresses your company owns and what runs on them.

steps.title: Ping sweep
steps.caption: The attacker sends small probe packets (ICMP echo) to every address in the range to learn which hosts are online.
steps.defender: The firewall sees quick, small probes to many addresses, including ones with no service. A burst of echoes to unused addresses is an early signal.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Port scan
steps.caption: The attacker sends connection attempts to many ports on the web server. Most are closed, but ports 80 and 443 answer, so they are marked as open.
steps.defender: Many SYN packets to different ports from one source is the classic port-scan pattern. The firewall log gives you source, target, ports, and the result.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Fingerprint services
steps.caption: The attacker reads the banners that open services return. The web server says it runs nginx 1.18, and the mail server answers as Postfix. Old versions help the attacker pick working exploits.
steps.defender: Web access logs show the scanner User-Agent. Keep vendor advisories on your watchlist so you know which versions in your estate are outdated.

steps.title: Probe other hosts
steps.caption: The attacker checks the mail server and one workstation address. Mail accepts connections on port 25. The workstation is blocked at the firewall, which means the segmentation is working.
steps.defender: A blocked scan is still a report. Confirm that the block was intended, and check why a workstation address is reachable enough to be probed at the edge.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Review findings
steps.caption: The attacker stops sending traffic and reviews the results: two live public servers, their open ports, and their software versions. The recon data is ready for the next step, usually vulnerability scanning.
steps.defender: The burst has ended, but the evidence stays in your logs. Hunt for other sources that scanned you the same way this month - one source is never alone.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: SOC investigates
steps.caption: An SOC analyst pulls the logs for the scanning IP, matches it against threat intelligence, and finds it is a known mass scanner. They confirm no other ports answered and no system was exploited.
steps.defender: Correlate the source with a scanner reputation feed. Then verify: did anything answer that should not have? Write down the source for future blocklists and reports.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Block and harden
steps.caption: The team blocks the scanning range at the firewall and reviews the exposed services. Blocking one IP will not stop the next scanner, so reducing the exposed surface matters more in the long run.
steps.defender: Treat this as a drill: it tested your logging, your alerting, and your asset inventory. Close what does not need to be public, and keep watching for new scanners.
